neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Mildly fatigued appearance. Normal language. Mildly slowed processing from chemotherapy-related fatigue.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right. Levator excursion left 7mm, right 10mm. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze (left eye complete at 50 seconds). Horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze. Limited left eye adduction. Pupils equal, reactive. Facial weakness bilateral. Voice nasal after sustained speech.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4/5. Distal strength intact. Deep tendon reflexes: 1+ throughout — mildly hyporeflexic (chemotherapy-related). Fatigable weakness documented on exam.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild stocking-glove diminished sensation feet (vincristine peripheral neuropathy).
neurological_exam.reflexes: 1+ throughout (mild hyporeflexia — vincristine neuropathy). Plantar downgoing.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly broad-based. Steppage pattern bilaterally (vincristine neuropathy).
neurological_exam.additional: NIF -48 cmH2O (borderline). No dysphagia currently. Mild jaw fatigue on eating. Oncology team suspected chemotherapy neurotoxicity — vincristine peripheral neuropathy confirmed but does not explain all findings.

patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia in a patient on chemotherapy for lymphoma
patient.history_present_illness: A 57-year-old man with high-grade peripheral T-cell lymphoma receiving EPOCH chemotherapy (after 4 of 6 planned cycles) presented with new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 5 weeks. He had been doing well on chemotherapy with near-complete metabolic response on interim PET-CT, but his oncology team noted new drooping of his left eyelid at a clinic visit. The patient confirmed the ptosis had been present for 5 weeks and was progressive. He developed horizontal diplopia 3 weeks ago, initially intermittent and worse after a long day, and now present during most of his waking hours. He also reported jaw fatigue when eating — he rested between bites during meal times. His voice had become increasingly nasal, a change his wife noted clearly. He denied significant dysphagia. He had been attributing all new neurological symptoms to chemotherapy toxicity, which had already caused peripheral neuropathy from vincristine. He had multiple prior episodes of febrile neutropenia requiring hospitalization and had a severe sepsis episode after his second cycle requiring one week in the ICU. His oncologist was concerned about: (1) central nervous system lymphoma invasion, (2) paraneoplastic syndrome, (3) chemotherapy neurotoxicity (vincristine-induced cranial neuropathy), and (4) opportunistic infection. Brain MRI was performed and reported as showing no CNS lymphoma. He was referred to neurology for NMJ evaluation after the oncologist noted the fatigable pattern was inconsistent with typical vincristine neuropathy, which causes peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy rather than cranial neuropathy with fatigability.

output.proposed: Pyridostigmine for MG in patient on vincristine-containing EPOCH chemotherapy
interactions: Vincristine is neurotoxic — causes peripheral neuropathy; does not directly worsen NMJ transmission
Pyridostigmine + vincristine: no significant pharmacokinetic interaction; both can affect neuromuscular function but via different mechanisms
contraindications: Avoid aminoglycosides — worsen MG (not in current chemotherapy regimen)
warnings: Vincristine neuropathy and MG coexist — clinical deterioration may reflect either vincristine toxicity progression or MG worsening; monitor both
EPOCH chemotherapy includes dexamethasone — steroid component may have partial MG benefit
If MG worsens significantly, consider IVIG rather than additional immunosuppression given active lymphoma treatment
Pyridostigmine cholinergic GI effects may worsen vincristine constipation — monitor carefully

output.query: Myasthenia gravis T-cell lymphoma paraneoplastic NMJ disorder association

results.title: Paraneoplastic NMJ disorders associated with hematologic malignancy
results.finding: Postsynaptic NMJ autoimmunity has been reported in association with non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes; anti-AChR antibodies can have a paraneoplastic origin; treatment of the underlying hematologic malignancy may improve neuromuscular symptoms, but concurrent chemotherapy-related axonal neuropathy (notably from vinca alkaloids) can complicate the clinical picture and should be evaluated as a separate process.

results.title: Anti-titin antibodies and thymoma vs paraneoplastic MG
results.finding: Anti-titin positive in MG can indicate thymoma OR paraneoplastic MG from other malignancies; CT chest should be performed but anti-titin alone does not confirm thymoma when CT is negative

output.summary: Paraneoplastic MG with anti-AChR antibodies has been reported in T-cell lymphoma and other non-SCLC malignancies. Anti-titin positive without CT-confirmed thymoma in a lymphoma patient is consistent with paraneoplastic mechanism. IVIG and pyridostigmine are appropriate; corticosteroids are problematic given lymphoma treatment. Lymphoma treatment remains priority.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), paraneoplastic in context of peripheral T-cell lymphoma; concurrent vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy as a separate process

differential.key_features: Vincristine can cause distal sensorimotor neuropathy but does NOT produce fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or RNS decrement; both processes coexist here.
Lymphomas are uncommon causes of LEMS; baseline CMAPs and high-rate RNS facilitation pattern would clarify; here AChR positive suggests MG.
Steroids in EPOCH could cause proximal myopathy but not fatigable bulbar weakness or RNS decrement.
Generalized fatigue from chemo is expected but does not produce focal fatigable cranial signs.
No mass lesion on brain MRI; CSF and imaging not supportive.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Perform single-fibre electromyography of a clinically weak muscle: the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test of neuromuscular-junction transmission, and the appropriate electrodiagnostic step when repetitive stimulation is normal or not available
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity and identify thymic abnormality on CT (here minimal residual mediastinal soft tissue from treated lymphoma — no thymoma)
Single-fiber EMG to confirm NMJ disorder distinct from chemotherapy neuropathy
Coordinate immunosuppression with oncology — patient is neutropenic and immunocompromised
Bedside FVC/NIF given cumulative chemotherapy and infection risk
Avoid further aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone exposure (relevant during febrile neutropenia episodes)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT use fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides during febrile neutropenia in this MG patient — substitute with non-NMJ-blocking agents.
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Vincristine peripheral neuropathy and MG are clinically distinguishable: vincristine → distal stocking-glove sensory loss; MG → fatigable proximal/bulbar weakness.
Active malignancy + immunosuppression: steroid-sparing strategies and infection control influence MG treatment selection.

red_herrings.data_point: Active peripheral T-cell lymphoma on EPOCH chemotherapy; multiple febrile neutropenia episodes; anti-titin positive
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute weakness to chemotherapy-induced fatigue, vincristine neuropathy, or lymphoma progression; anti-titin attributed to thymoma when no thymoma is present.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia with RNS decrement and AChR positivity = MG; vincristine neuropathy is a separate concurrent process; anti-titin can be positive in late-onset MG without thymoma.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute weakness/dyspnea to anemia; ignore MG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild cytopenias are expected on EPOCH and do not explain fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness; MG workup is separately indicated.

actions_withdrawn.reason: The bedside ice-pack test is recommended here but its result is not stored in this case, or in any case in the condition — the only mention of it anywhere is this recommendation. Its outcome does not follow from the documented ptosis, and at roughly 80% sensitivity it is not definitional of the diagnosis, so authoring a result would be inventing one.
